coredata.dc:description: Obesity triggers numerous other disorders, such as type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD). Endocrine Disrupting Chemicals (EDC) such as Bisphenol A (BPA) have obesogenic effects, which have been replaced by Bisphenol S (BPS). The chronicity of obesity and MASLD, as well as BPS exposure, compromises Mitochondrial Biogenesis (MBG) and triggers the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. Therefore, this study aims to investigate whether BPS exposure affects hepatic morphology, MBG, and ER stress pathways in the liver in male mice fed a standard and high-fat diet. C57BL/6 adult male mice were fed a control (SC) or high fat (HF) diet for 12 weeks and exposed or not to BPS (25 μg/kg of body mass/day) by drinking water. The animals were divided into a control diet not exposed to BPS (SCD), a control diet exposed to BPS (SCDB), a high-fat diet not exposed to BPS (HFD), and a high-fat diet exposed to BPS (HFDB) for 12 weeks. Body mass, glucose, and lipid profile were evaluated. In the liver, morphology and lipid metabolism, ER stress, and MBG markers were assessed. Data were presented as mean ± standard deviation and analyzed by one-way ANOVA, followed by the Holm-Sidak post-test. p < 0.05 was considered significant. BPS exposure led to increased body mass, and disrupted lipid and glucose metabolism, leading to alterations in hepatic mitochondrial dynamics, ER stress, and compromised hepatic structural support. The combination with a high-fat diet augmented insulin levels disrupted cholesterol metabolism, and compromised mitochondrial and endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis, resulting in more severe structural damage. In conclusion, BPS was able to facilitate the development of obesity and increase the risk of manifesting associated comorbidities when combined with a high-fat diet.

ce:section.ce:para: Obesity has reached pandemic scales over the last decades and its growing prevalence poses a big threat to public health systems worldwide. In 2022, approximately 2.5 billion adults worldwide were overweight, with 890 million of them being obese (Ritchie & Roser, 2017; World Health Organization, 2024). The burden of obesity falls mainly on its association with a wide variety of diseases, such as type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD), and other metabolic disorders. The MASLD encloses a spectrum of liver disorders that range from steatosis up to steatohepatitis with lobular inflammation, liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, or even hepatocellular carcinoma. A bigger concern regarding MASLD is its elevated prevalence, broadly justified by its strong association with obesity. Around 70–80 % of individuals with obesity are likely to develop MASLD and its worldwide prevalence is estimated at around 25 % in the general population (Mitra et al., 2020; Polyzos et al., 2019; Younossi et al., 2016).

As MASLD progresses, the function and integrity of organelles such as mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) are disrupted. In the early stages of the disease, mitochondria enter a state of flexibility between fusion and fission processes, known as Mitochondrial Biogenesis (MBG). As the disease progresses, mitochondrial fission increases while fusion tends to decrease (Longo et al., 2021). Uncontrolled mitochondrial fission promotes liver fibrosis, besides its reduction alters the expression of lipid metabolism genes and alleviates hepatic steatosis (Galloway et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2020). On the other hand, hyperlipidemic diets and MASLD decrease the expression of proteins involved in the mitochondrial fusion process (F. Gong et al., 2019; Hernández-Alvarez et al., 2019; Tong et al., 2016). Thus, the investigation of mitochondrial dynamics becomes crucial for understanding the progression of MASLD.

ER dysfunction during MASLD leads to the accumulation of misfolded proteins within the lumen, resulting in ER stress. To restore organelle homeostasis, the Unfolded Protein Response (UPR) is activated through transmembrane stress transducer proteins, including Inositol-Requiring Enzyme 1α (IRE1α), Protein Kinase R-Like ER Kinase (PERK) and Activating Transcription Factor 6 (ATF6). Each of these proteins initiates distinct signaling cascades to manage ER stress and attempt to restore normal cellular function. Under normal conditions, these transmembrane proteins are associated with the 78 kDa Glucose-Regulated Chaperone Protein (GRP78), which is released from the ER during MASLD progression (Chen et al., 2020; Sepúlveda-Fragoso et al., 2021).

In the context of obesity as a multifactorial disease, it is well established that many environmental aspects may contribute to its development, including environmental pollutants. These pollutants may be classified as Endocrine Disrupting Chemicals (EDC) (Gore et al., 2015; Grün & Blumberg, 2009; Lin & Li, 2021), and among these are bisphenols, which integrate polycarbonate plastics. Bisphenol A (BPA) has been the largest used bisphenol throughout the years; however, in response to well-consolidated evidence pointing to its endocrine-disrupting effects, governments worldwide have regulated and restricted its production (Catenza et al., 2021; Cimmino et al., 2020). Bisphenol S (BPS) is the main substitute for BPA and has a similar chemical structure. It is broadly present in the food and consumables industries, although there are no regulations or restrictions over its production and usage (Brulport et al., 2020; Thoene et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2018).

The literature already reports a correlation between BPS and obesity, along with potential mechanisms contributing to its development and associated comorbidities, such as MASLD, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance (Chi et al., 2024; P. Gong et al., 2023; Varghese & Hall, 2023). High consumption of lipid-rich diets contributes to the development of obesity, metabolic disorders and the pathological changes observed in MASLD, such as intrahepatic lipid accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction and ER stress (Lian et al., 2020). However, there is limited knowledge regarding its association with BPS exposure in the development and progression of obesity and MASLD, particularly with respect to the imbalance of mitochondrial and ER function. Studies have shown that long-term exposure to BPS can increase the expression of proteins involved in mitochondrial fission and the UPR-PERK pathway (Azevedo et al., 2019; Qin et al., 2020). Nonetheless, it is still necessary to better elucidate these pathways when BPS exposure is associated with a high-fat diet.

Thus, our objective was to evaluate how both interventions affect the metabolism of mice, focusing on liver morphology and hepatic MBG and ER stress pathways. We hypothesized that the combination leads to a significant dysregulation of glucose and lipid metabolism, and alterations in liver morphology, compared to each exposure in isolation.

Adult male C57BL/6 mice (3 months old) were housed in propylene cages under controlled conditions of temperature (22 ± 2 °C), humidity (60 ± 10 %), and lighting (12 h light-dark cycle), with ad libitum access to food and water. The experimental protocols adhered to the “”Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (National Institutes of Health, 2011 - revised in 1996, EUA) guidelines. The study and procedures were approved by the Ethics Committee for Animal Use (CEUA) at the Federal Fluminense University (CEUA, 1929240521).

The animals were divided into four groups (n = 12/group) at the onset of the experimental protocol, as follows: a) SCD: animals fed a standard chow diet; b) SCDB: animals fed a standard chow diet and exposed to BPS; c) HFD: animals fed a high-fat diet; and d) HFDB: animals fed a high-fat diet and exposed to BPS; for 12 weeks. The diets were produced by PragSoluções, following AIN-93-M specification (Reeves et al., 1993). The standard chow diet contained 76 % carbohydrate, 14 % protein, 10 % fat, and a total energy of 15 kJ/g, while the high-fat diet presented 36 % carbohydrate, 14 % protein, and 50 % fat, with a total energy of 21 kJ/g. BPS (Sigma-Aldrich, Milwaukee, WI, USA) was diluted in absolute ethanol (0.1 %) and administered through drinking water at a dose of 25 μg/kg of body mass/day, in glass bottles. To maintain a consistent dosage, weekly calculations of the BPS concentration in each bottle were performed based on the average body mass and water intake per cage. The mean BPS intake was 29.3 ± 4.40 μg/kg/day (Alexandre-Santos et al., 2024). For the animals not exposed to BPS, absolute ethanol (0.1 %) was added to their drinking water under the same conditions as the glass bottles. The established dose was in accordance with No Observed Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL) concentrations for systemic toxicity determined through rodent studies, estimated at 60 mg/kg/day (https://echa.europa.eu). To analyze the impact of a lower dose and in the absence of specific BPS regulation, half of the tolerable daily intake of BPA was considered (50 μg/kg of body mass/day) (https://www.fda.gov/), along with the maximum migration limit of BPS in food (50 μg/L) (Xie et al., 2025).

Throughout the experimental protocol, body mass (kg) was assessed weekly (n = 12/group), while food (g) and energy (kJ) intake were measured daily (n = 12/group). Body mass gain was calculated using the formula: Δ = [Final body mass (g) - Initial body mass (g)]. Food intake was monitored daily by measuring the amount of diet provided (g) and subtracting the leftover from the previous day. Energy intake was calculated using the formula: [food intake (g/day/animal) x dietary energy content (SC: 15 kJ/g; HF: 21 kJ/g)]. Water intake was monitored three times a week (on alternate days) by measuring the amount of water (mL) provided and subtracting the leftover (n = 12/group). Food, energy and water intakes were presented as the average for each cage per week throughout the entire experimental protocol period. The BPS dose in the water was adjusted according to the water intake and body mass.

The Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) was performed in the 11th week of the experimental protocol (n = 5/group). Fasting blood glucose was measured after 6 h of fasting, followed by administration of glucose (1.0 g/kg), via orogastric gavage. Glucose levels were then assessed using a manual glucometer (Johnson&Johnson, New Brunswick, NJ, USA) at 15, 30, 60, and 120 min thereafter, via a small incision on the animal's tail to access the caudal vein (Magliano et al., 2013). The values were presented as the mean of all animals in the group.

At the end of the 12-weeks experimental protocol, the animals underwent a 6-h fasting period followed by heparinization and administration of ketamine (40 mg/kg) and xylazine (8 mg/kg), via intraperitoneal, for euthanasia by exsanguination. The blood was collected via cardiac puncture, centrifuged to obtain plasma (20 min at room temperature), and stored in a −80 °C freezer for plasma analyses.

The liver was carefully dissected, weighted, and photographed for macroscopic observation (n = 12/group). One part was fixed in 10 % formalin (1.27 mol/L in 0,1 M phosphate buffer, pH 7.2) for histological analyses, while the other part was frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored in a −80 °C freezer for molecular analyses.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Plasma analyses and hepatic lipid content
ce:section.ce:para: The plasma and hepatic cholesterol and triglycerides concentrations were determined in triplicate using enzymatic colorimetric methods (Bioclin System II, Belo Horizonte, MG, Brazil) and automatic spectrophotometric reading (n = 5/group). According to the specifications of the kits, cholesterol concentrations were measured by reacting with Lipoprotein Lipase, Cholesterol Oxidase, Phenol, 4-Aminoantipyrine, and Peroxidase, with readings taken at 505 nm. The triglycerides concentrations were measured by reacting with Lipoprotein Lipase, Glycerol Kinase, Glycerol-3-Phosphate Oxidase, 4-Aminoantipyrine, 4-Chlorophenol, and Peroxidase, with readings taken at 505 nm. Fasting insulin levels were measured through an Elisa kit designed for mice (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and an automatic spectrophotometer (n = 5/group). The samples were read at 450 nm and calculated using a standard curve. HOMA-IR index was calculated using the formula: [fasting glucose of OGTT (mmol/L) x fasting insulin (μUI/mL)]/22.5 (Matthews et al., 1985), while the cholesterol vLDL was determined using the formula: [triglycerides (mg/dL)]/5 (n = 5/group) (Friedewald et al., 1972).

The liver underwent routine histological processing and was sectioned into 5 μm thick sections, after fixation in 10 % formalin. Hematoxylin and Eosin (HE) staining was performed for stereological analyses (Catta-Preta et al., 2011), and Gomori silver impregnation was executed for reticular fiber estimation. Fifteen digital photomicrographs (Leica DM500, Wetzlar, Germany) of random fields per animal were obtained for hepatic stereology (n = 5/group). The images were analyzed using a 36-point test system by STEPanizer software to determine the volume density of hepatic steatosis (Vv) and quantify the macro and microvesicular profiles (Qa). Steatosis volume density was estimated through the ratio of partial points that touch the fat droplets (PP) to the total points (TP): Vv = PP/36 (%) (Aguila et al., 2003). Additionally, the profiles were evaluated based on the number of hepatocytes that exhibited macro and microvesicular steatosis within a known area, excluding those that intersected the “restricted lines''. This was determined using the formula: (count structures quantity)/(test area) (%) (Magliano et al., 2013).

Reticular fibers were analyzed through the 64-point test system by STEPanizer software, where ten random digital photomicrographs were evaluated per animal (n = 5/group). The area of reticular fibers was estimated through the ratio of PP that touch the reticular fiber to the TP: Vv = PP/64 (%).

Approximately 70 mg of the liver (n = 5/group) was used for protein extraction with RIPA lysis buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. The samples were applied in 8–15 % polyacrylamide gel and separated by electrophoresis, in accordance with the protein molecular weight. After transferring the gel samples to a polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membrane (Amersham Biosciences, Piscataway, NJ, USA), it was blocked with albumin and then incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies targeting: a) lipid metabolism: Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptor Gamma (PPAR-ɣ), Sterol Regulatory Element-Binding Protein 1c (SREBP-1c), and Sterol Regulatory Element-Binding Protein 2 (SREBP-2); b) glucose metabolism: Glucose-6-Phosphatase (G6Pase); c) antioxidant system: Nuclear Factor Erythroid 2-Related Factor 2 (NRF2); d) MBG - regulator: Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptor Gamma Coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1ɑ); fission: Dynamin-Related Protein 1 (DRP1), Mitochondrial Fission Factor (MFF), and Fission 1 (FIS1); fusion: Optic Atrophy 1 (OPA1), and Mitofusin 2 (MFN2); e) ER stress: 78 kDa Glucose-Regulated Chaperone Protein (GRP78), Activating Transcription Factor 4 (ATF4), and C/EBP Homologous Protein (CHOP) (Table S1). After the primary antibody, the membrane was incubated with a biotinylated secondary antibody (Novus Biological, Centennial, CO, USA) followed by streptavidin (Vector Laboratories, Newark, CA, USA). The protein expression was detected by chemiluminescence using ECL and band images were obtained with the ChemiDoc system of molecular images (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA). Band intensity was quantified using ImageJ software, version 1.44 (NIH, imagej. nih.gov/ij, USA), and corrected by the loading control cyclophilin (Hnasko & Hnasko, 2015).

The data underwent testing for normal distribution curve and variance homoscedasticity, and are presented as mean ± standard deviation. Group differences were assessed using a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by the Holm-Sidak post-test. Analysis and graphs were generated using GraphPad Prism (version 8.0, La Jolla, CA, USA). A significance level of p < 0.05 was applied in all cases.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Body mass gain, and food, energy, and water intake
ce:section.ce:para: The BPS increased body mass in control mice (+69 %, p < 0.01) and, as expected, the high-fat diet promoted body mass gain in the HFD and HFDB in comparison to the SCD (+330 %, p < 0.0001; +297 %, p < 0.0001, respectively) and SCDB (+154 %, p < 0.0001; +135 %, p < 0.0001, respectively) groups. Furthermore, the high-fat groups exhibited lower food and water intake but demonstrated higher energy consumption in relation to the SCD and SCDB (p < 0.05) groups (Table 1 ).

OGTT curve revealed higher area under the curve (AUC) in all experimental groups when compared to the SCD group (SCDB: +8 %, p < 0.05; HFD: +37 %, p < 0.0001; HFDB: +42 %, p < 0.0001), and in the high-fat groups in relation to the SCDB group (HFD: +27 %, p < 0.01; HFDB: +32 %, p < 0.001). Similar differences were also observed in fasting blood glucose levels (p < 0.05) (Fig. 1 ).

Insulin concentration was elevated in SCDB (+104 %, p < 0.05), HFD (+100 %, p < 0.05), and HFDB (+189 %, p < 0.0001) groups in relation to the SCD group. Furthermore, the HOMA-IR presented higher values in these same groups (SCDB: +112 %, p < 0.01; HFD: +136 %, p < 0.01; HFDB: +266 %, p < 0.0001). Interestingly, the combination of BPS with a high-fat diet was able to induce higher insulin concentration (+42 %, p < 0.05; +73 %, p < 0.001; respectively) and HOMA-IR compared to the SCDB (+44 %, p < 0.05) and HFD (+55 %, p < 0.01) groups (Table 2 ).

Hepatic analyses of glucose metabolism revealed an increase in G6Pase expression in all experimental groups in relation to the SCD group (SCDB: +116 %, p < 0.05; HFD: +123 %, p < 0.01; HFDB: +136 %, p < 0.01) (Fig. 2 . D).

Plasma triglycerides concentration was higher in the high-fat groups compared to the SCD (HFD: +34 %, p < 0.01; HFDB: +35 %, p < 0.01, respectively) and SCDB (HFD: +35 %, p < 0.01; HFDB: +36 %, p < 0.01) groups (Table 2). However, in the liver, the effects of BPS were evident in the SCDB (+93 %, p < 0.01) group compared to the control group, besides greater accumulation in high-fat groups (HFD: +90 %, p < 0.01; HFDB: +85 %, p < 0.01) (Table 3 ).

All experimental groups exhibited higher concentrations in relation to the SCD group regarding plasma cholesterol (SCDB: +39 %, p < 0.01; HFD: +93 %, p < 0.0001; HFDB: +65 %, p < 0.0001) and vLDL (SCDB: +33 %, p < 0.05; HFD: +77 %, p < 0.0001; HFDB: +96 %, p < 0.0001). Similarly, the HFD (cholesterol: +38 %, p < 0.0001; vLDL: +34 %, p < 0.01) and HFDB (cholesterol: +18 %, p < 0.05; vLDL: +48 %, p < 0.0001) groups had comparable results to the SCDB group. Interestingly, the HFDB group showed a 14 % reduction in plasma cholesterol compared to the HFD group (p < 0.05) (Table 2). Hepatic cholesterol followed a similar pattern the SCDB, HFD and HFDB groups had increased levels compared to the SCD group (SCDB: +38 %, p < 0.001; HFD: +37 %, p < 0.001; HFDB: +22 %, p < 0.01), and HFDB group had lower concentrations in relation to the SCDB (−12 %, p < 0.05) and HFD (−11 %, p < 0.05) groups (Table 3).

Molecular analyses of hepatic lipid metabolism revealed increased protein expression of PPAR˗γ (SCDB: +87 %, p < 0.05; HFD: +174 %, p < 0.001; HFDB: +111 %, p < 0.05), SREBP-1c (SCDB: +166 %, p < 0.001; HFD: +197 %, p < 0.0001; HFDB: +163 %, p < 0.001) and SREBP-2 (SCDB: +33 %, p < 0.05; HFD: +45 %, p < 0.001; HFDB: +55 %, p < 0.001) in all experimental groups compared to the SCD group. Additionally, PPAR˗γ expression was significantly higher in the HFD (+46 %, p < 0.05) and HFDB (+27 %, p < 0.05) groups than in the SCDB group, while the SREBP-2 expression was greater in animals of the HFDB group compared to those of the SCDB group (+16 %, p < 0.05) (Fig. 2).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Liver mass, lipid content, and morphology
ce:section.ce:para: The absolute liver mass was increased in the SCDB (+21 %, p < 0.05), HFD (+39 %, p < 0.001), and HFDB (+25 %, p < 0.01) groups in comparison to the SCD group, and similar findings were observed in lipid content and hepatic histology (Table 3). These groups showed a greater concentration of hepatic triglycerides (SCDB: +93 %, p < 0.01; HFD: +90 %, p < 0.01; HFDB: +85 %, p < 0.01) and cholesterol (SCDB: +38 %, p < 0.001; HFD: +37 %, p < 0.001; HFDB: +22 %, p < 0.01), as well as a higher percentage of the total (SCDB: +297 %, p < 0.01; HFD: +599 %, p < 0.0001; HFDB: +509 %, p < 0.0001), macrovesicular (SCDB: +241 %, p < 0.001; HFD: +338 %, p < 0.0001; HFDB: +346 %, p < 0.0001) and microvesicular steatosis (SCDB: +241 %, p < 0.001; HFD: +338 %, p < 0.0001; HFDB: +346 %, p < 0,0001), which is reflected in organ macroscopy (Table 3 and Fig. 3 ). Moreover, there was a 43 % decrease of reticular fiber in the SCDB group (p < 0.05), 52 % in the HFD group (p < 0.01), and 66 % in the HFDB group (p < 0.01) compared to the SCD group (Table 3 and Fig. 3, B).

Furthermore, the high-fat groups exhibited a higher percentage of total (HFD: +76 %, p < 0.01; HFDB: +53 %, p < 0.05) and microvesicular (HFD: +28 %, p < 0.05; HFDB: +31 %, p < 0.05) steatosis in relation to the SCDB group. Additionally, the HFDB group demonstrated a reduction in cholesterol levels compared to the SCDB (−12 %, p < 0.05) and HFD (−11 %, p < 0.05) groups and in reticular fibers in relation to the SCDB group (−40 %, p < 0.05) (Table 3 and Fig. 3, B).

The antioxidant system represented by NRF2 showed lower expression levels in the HFD (−50 %, p < 0.05) and HFDB (−48 %, p < 0.05) groups compared to the SCD group (Fig. 4 , A). A similar pattern was observed for PGC˗1ɑ expression, the main regulator of MBG (HFD: 20 %, p < 0.05; HFDB: 30 %, p < 0.05), which also presented a decrease in expression in the animals of the HFDB group in relation to those of the SCDB (−27 %, p < 0.05) and HFD (−13 %, p < 0.01) groups (Fig. 4, B).

In the mitochondrial fission process, DRP1 and MFF expression was increased in the SCDB (+20 %, p < 0.05; +85 %, p < 0.05; respectively), HFD (+24 %, p < 0.05; +130 %, p < 0.01; respectively) and HFDB (+56 %, p < 0.0001; +268 %, p < 0.0001; respectively) groups compared to the SCD group. Interestingly, these proteins also exhibited higher expression in the HFDB group in relation to SCDB (DRP1: +30 %, p < 0.01; MFF: +99 %, p < 0.0001) and HFD (DRP1: +25 %, p < 0.01; MFF: +60 %, p < 0.001) groups (Fig. 4C and D). Additionally, a greater FIS1 expression was demonstrated in all experimental groups (SCDB: +188 %, p < 0.0001; HFD: +41 %, p < 0.05; HFDB: +146 %, p < 0.0001) compared to the SCD group, and in the BPS exposed groups in relation to the high-fat group (SCDB: +51 %, p < 0.0001; HFDB: +75 %, p < 0.01) (Fig. 4, E).

In the mitochondrial fusion process, OPA1, responsible for merging the inner mitochondrial membranes, had a lower expression in the HFD and HFDB groups in relation to SCD (−30 %, p < 0.01; −47 %, p < 0.0001; respectively) and SCDB groups (−18 %, p < 0.05; −38 %, p < 0.01; respectively), with a reduction also observed in the HFDB group relative to the HFD group (−24 %, p < 0.01) (Fig. 4, F). Interestingly, MFN2, associated with merging the outer mitochondrial membranes, had a higher expression in all experimental groups compared to the SCD group (SCDB: +72 %, p < 0.05; HFD: +150 %, p < 0.01; HFDB: +204 %, p < 0.0001), and high-fat groups in relation to the SCDB group (HFD: +45 %, p < 0.05; HFDB: +77 %, p < 0.01) (Fig. 4, G).

To assess the balance between mitochondrial fission and fusion, the ratio of the main proteins involved in these processes, DRP1 and OPA1, respectively, was calculated. Upon evaluating the results, all interventions were found to increase hepatic mitochondrial fission compared to the SCD group (SCDB: +39 %, p < 0.05; HFD: +73 %, p < 0.001; HFDB: +188 %, p < 0.0001). Furthermore, an increase in this process was observed in the hyperlipidemic groups compared to the SCDB group (HFD: +25 %, p < 0.05; HFDB: +108 %, p < 0.0001) and in the animals of the HFD group compared to those of the HFDB group (+67 %, p < 0.0001) (Fig. 4, H).

GRP78, ATF4 and CHOP showed an increase of their expression in the SCDB (GRP78: +147 %, p < 0.05; ATF4: +85 %, p < 0.05; CHOP: +50 %, p < 0.05) HFD (+163 %, p < 0.05; ATF4: +209 %, p < 0.05; CHOP: +76 %, p < 0.01) and HFDB (+289 %, p < 0.001; ATF4: +297 %, p < 0.01; CHOP: +109 %, p < 0.001) groups compared to the SCD group. Furthermore, these proteins presented a higher expression in the HFDB group in relation to the SCDB group (GRP78: +57 %, p < 0.05; ATF4: +115 %, p < 0.05; CHOP: +39 %, p < 0.05) (Fig. 5 ).

In the present study, BPS exposure resulted in body mass gain in animals consuming the SC diet, highlighting its obesogenic effects. This finding aligned with previous research demonstrating that BPS stimulates lipid synthesis and storage through exacerbated activation of PPAR-γ (Ahmed & Atlas, 2016; Mornagui et al., 2023). Nevertheless, this effect was not observed when comparing the group exposed to the lipid-rich diet and BPS with the group fed only the HF diet, despite evidence that lower doses of BPS (1.5 μg/kg of body weight/day) over prolonged periods (gestation, lactation, and post-weaning) can induce body mass gain in diet-induced obese mice (Brulport et al., 2021; Ivry Del Moral et al., 2016). Conversely, Ahn et al. (2020) reported a tendency for reduced body mass in the same experimental model of the present study, but exposed to higher doses (50 and 500 μg/kg of body weight/day) of BPS during the prenatal period and fed a HF diet starting at 6 months of age (Ahn et al., 2020). These findings suggest that the tendency to reduce body mass gain in diet-induced obese mice exposed to 25 μg/kg of body mass/day (a dose not widely studied) is consistent with the literature, as BPS does not exhibit a monotonic response. This indicates that some of its effects are more pronounced at lower doses than at higher ones, in this case when combined with a HF diet (Lagarde et al., 2015).

In the glucose metabolism, the animals in the SCDB group exhibited higher AUC, fasting blood glucose of OGTT and insulin levels, highlighting the presence of insulin resistance, as represented by the greater HOMA-IR index. This may be attributed to the effects of BPS on genes and enzymes involved in gluconeogenesis. Some studies have demonstrated that BPS influences the expression of mediators associated with hepatic gluconeogenesis, including G6Pase (Rezg et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2018). Consistent with these findings, the present study revealed that BPS similarly influences the expression of this enzyme in the liver, potentially driving hepatic glucose synthesis and subsequent metabolic dysfunctions. Others mechanisms are involved in the course of insulin resistance, such as insulin receptor and pancreatic β-cells dysfunction, chronic inflammation and ectopic lipid accumulation, which impact glucose metabolism, endoplasmic reticulum stress, mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress (Lee et al., 2022; Petersen & Shulman, 2018). BPS also has the ability to elevate plasma insulin levels can be explained by its estrogenic activity on pancreatic β-cells, similar to BPA. These cells express estrogen receptors that stimulate insulin release when activated. Consequently, the estrogenic action of bisphenols stimulates insulin secretion (Alonso-Magdalena et al., 2006; Pérez-Bermejo et al., 2021). Interestingly, the combination of BPS exposure with a HF diet worsens insulin resistance, by increase in fasting insulin levels and HOMA-IR. A similar outcome was observed in studies using different doses of BPA combined with a HF diet, indicating a comparable effect on insulin levels for both compounds in association with the diet. The authors highlighted the action of BPA on oxidative stress and inflammation markers, which could contribute to the insulin resistance (X. Hong et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2014). These findings highlight that the impact of BPS on insulin secretion and sensitivity is significantly impaired by the HF diet.

Upon examining the lipid metabolism of the animals, BPS unleashed an increase in plasma concentrations of total cholesterol and vLDL. Li et al. (2019) observed that adult male C57BL/6 mice exposed to 50 and 500 μg/kg/day of BPA exhibited high serum and intrahepatic cholesterol concentrations. The author explains that this EDC impairs cholesterol metabolism with the increase of SREBP-2 expression in the liver, which promotes cholesterol synthesis and deposition within the organ (Horn et al., 2022; Q. Li et al., 2019). In the present study, assessment of hepatic SREBP-2 expression revealed that BPS exacerbates its activity, which accounts for the increased plasma and hepatic cholesterol levels. Interestingly, the association of BPS with a HF diet demonstrated a reduction in both serum and hepatic cholesterol concentrations compared to animals exposed only to the HF diet, a finding also observed in the male first-generation mice of Brulport et al. (2021) study (Brulport et al., 2021).

Alongside SREBP2-mediated cholesterol accumulation, BPS hyperactivation of SREBP1c - a key regulator involved in lipogenesis de novo and triglycerides synthesis pathway - also contributes to the steatotic liver (Horn et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2020). In agreement with these findings, literature shows that BPS upregulates hepatic MCT1, which leads to higher pyruvate content and consequently increased gluconeogenesis and ATP synthesis. Both processes inhibit AMPK phosphorylation, enhancing the activation of SREBP1 (Mornagui et al., 2022). BPS has also been revealed to inhibit lipophagy through upregulation of PPARα, leading to lipid accumulation (Liang et al., 2023). It is important to note that liver steatosis is a complex disorder with multiple synergistic mechanisms.

The increase in intrahepatic cholesterol and triglycerides is evidenced by the formation of macro- and microvesicular steatotic droplets, which were more prevalent in the SCDB, HFD, and HFDB groups compared to the SCD group. It is important to note that the percentage of microvesicles was higher than that of macrovesicles in these groups. The literature has long considered microvesicular steatosis potentially harmful due to its association with impaired mitochondrial β-oxidation, which reduces the esterification of free fatty acids and their subsequent deposition (Day & James, 1998; Fromenty & Pessayre, 1995). However, recent studies suggest that microvesicles represent an intermediate stage in the development of macrovesicles, reflecting the progression of MASLD (Kristiansen et al., 2019; Tandra et al., 2011). Interestingly, the concomitant exposure to BPS and a HF diet did not worsen the hepatic steatosis in the HFDB group. Research combining BPS exposure with HF diets remains limited in the literature. However, intra-hepatic lipid deposition might manifest after a longer exposure period to both the EDC and the HF diet, and/or at different doses than those analyzed in this study (Marchlewicz et al., 2022; Strakovsky et al., 2015). In addition, BPS induced the loss of hepatic reticular fibers, and its combined effect with a HF diet exacerbated this result. These fibers are essential for supporting the components of the hepatic lobule and the extracellular matrix. The extracellular matrix integrity relies on a balance between its degradation and synthesis, managed by matrix metalloproteinases and their tissue inhibitors, respectively. Disruption of this balance, such as in the presence of Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS), interrupts extracellular matrix maintenance, leading to architectural loss and progression of liver injury (Wen et al., 2016).

The accumulation of intrahepatic lipids due to impaired elimination intensifies mitochondrial β-oxidation, resulting in increased synthesis of ROS. Elevated levels of these compounds cause mitochondrial DNA damage, disrupting the encoding of proteins essential for mitochondrial metabolism. These include NRF2, a critical component of the antioxidant defense system, and PGC-1ɑ, the master regulator of MBG, which interacts with NRF2 to maintain mitochondrial homeostasis (Chen et al., 2020; Kuchay et al., 2020; Popov, 2020; Ryoo & Kwak, 2018). The present study observed a decline in the expression of NRF2 and PGC-1ɑ in HFD groups, and further demonstrated that BPS exacerbated the reduction in their expression. Some studies suggest that bisphenols induce ROS synthesis and inhibit the expression of NRF2, along with antioxidant enzymes and genes, leading to oxidative stress (Mohammed et al., 2020; Müller et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2023). Regarding PGC-1ɑ, no significant difference was observed between the SCDB and SCD groups. According to Azevedo et al. (2019), a difference might be observed if the experimental protocol was longer (38 weeks) and/or if a higher dose (50 μg/kg body weight/day) were administered (Azevedo et al., 2019). However, it was evident that chronic exposure to BPS and the HF diet worsened PGC-1α expression in the liver. As previously mentioned, there are few studies on high-fat diet fed mice exposed to BPS, making this the first to report such findings. The regulation of PGC-1ɑ in MBG is observed in the balance between mitochondrial fission and fusion. Disruptions in these mitochondrial dynamics are known to occur in the MASLD, leading to increased expression of proteins involved in fission and decreased expression of those involved in the fusion process (R. Li et al., 2020; Longo et al., 2021; Popov, 2020). In the present study BPS exposure increased the expression of FIS1, MFF and DRP1, a key inducer of mitochondrial fission, besides reducing the expression of OPA1, responsible for the fusion of inner mitochondrial membranes and the maintenance of mitochondrial dynamics. These findings are consistent with a recent study that showed that Bisphenol F increased lipid deposition and mitochondrial dysfunction in the liver (Zhang et al., 2023). Interestingly, the concomitant exposure to BPS and HF diet exacerbated these differences. Despite the controversy compared to OPA1, the BPS chronic exposure increased MFN2 expression, which could be explained by role outside of MBG. Bassot et al. (2021) explain that the overexpression of this protein promotes the accumulation of intrahepatic triglycerides due to inefficient excretion, which clarifies why plasma triglyceride levels did not increase in animals exposed solely to BPS, even though hepatic triglyceride levels are elevated. Additionally, MFN2 overexpression induces a reduction in the size of the steatotic vesicles and, along with cholesterol depletion, promotes the association between ER and mitochondrial membranes (Bassot et al., 2021; de Brito & Scorrano, 2008; Fujimoto et al., 2012). It is suggested that this increase in membrane associations disrupts mitochondrial dynamics and promotes ER stress, with these effects being further intensified by reduced cholesterol levels.

The ER is another organelle affected by intrahepatic lipid accumulation, leading to the misfolding of proteins that accumulate within its lumen, triggering the ER stress (Chen et al., 2020; Sepúlveda-Fragoso et al., 2021). In the animals studied, BPS induced activation of the PERK pathway with significant involvement in the expression of GRP78, ATF4 and CHOP. Previous studies using different experimental models and dosages of BPS and BPA have reported the disruption caused by bisphenols in the hepatic ER. Hong et al. (2023) observed that exposure to a high dose of BPA (100 μg/kg/day) activated PERK pathway in male C57BL/6 J mice, a finding similar to the effects reported Quin et al. (2020), where zebrafish exposed to various doses of BPS (1, 10 and 100 μg/L) also exhibited activation of this pathway. Both studies highlighted the disruption of homeostasis in hepatic lipid metabolism and the hyperactivation of the PERK pathway caused by bisphenols, leading to ER stress (L. Hong et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2020). The present study also observed that the HF diet intensified the effect of BPS, leading to a further increase in GRP78, ATF4 and CHOP expression. This was highlighted by the differences evidenced between the HFDB and SCDB groups.

Although an increase in body mass and higher plasma concentrations of glucose and lipids were observed in the group exposed only to BPS, these differences were not demonstrated in the HFDB group compared to those fed only the high-fat diet. It is suggested that the high lipid content of the diet may reach a damage threshold, thereby mitigating the deleterious effects previously attributed to BPS. Therefore, a diet with lower lipid-derived caloric content or alternative energy sources, such as carbohydrates, may be more suitable for evaluating the combined effects of dietary intake and BPS exposure. Another factor to consider is the duration of the experimental protocol. The results might have become apparent if the duration had exceeded the 12 weeks applied in the present study.

The results indicate that exposure to BPS alone triggers body mass gain, disrupts glucose and lipid metabolism, and causes liver damage. This damage includes increased hepatic steatosis, disruption of mitochondrial dynamics, induction of ER stress, besides deterioration of hepatic structural support with the loss of reticular fibers. All these results suggest the capability of BPS to facilitate the development of obesity and its associated comorbidities, such as MASLD.

Furthermore, when combined with a high-fat diet, BPS exacerbates insulin levels, disrupts cholesterol metabolism, and compromises mitochondrial and ER homeostasis in the liver, resulting in more severe structural damage. Thus, the association of these interventions significantly elevates the risk of developing the comorbidities.
